text: Chapter One gave you the vocabulary — sensitive data, PII, the major regulations. This chapter turns that vocabulary into something you can actually apply: data classification.

Data classification is sorting data into a small number of sensitivity tiers, so handling rules — who can access it, whether it's encrypted, how long it's kept — attach to the label automatically, instead of being decided case by case, every single time.

Without classification you're stuck choosing between two bad options: protect everything at the highest level, which is safe but wildly expensive, or protect everything lightly, which is cheap but leaves your most sensitive data exposed. Classification lets you right-size controls to actual risk.

This is where Chapter One's ideas stop being abstract. 'This data is sensitive' becomes a label — Confidential, Restricted — stamped on an actual table. 'This table has PII under GDPR' becomes a concrete rule a system can enforce. The label is the bridge from policy to practice.

Four lessons left in this chapter: the actual schemes and labels organizations use next, then discovering sensitive data in the first place, then applying classifications to real systems, then classification governance. Next lesson: the common tiers, and what distinguishes each one.
